title: Decimal and percent summit
summary: Teach the family one proof from last week, then climb a three-peak summit over the hardest decimal, fraction and percent ideas so far.

steps.title: Teach the family one proof
steps.body:
Before you start the check, go back to the pigeonhole or parity puzzle you invented last week. Present it to your family like a scientist presenting a proof, not a puzzle: state the claim, let them guess whether it is true, then show why it has to be true, not just true for the examples you tried.

Name the idea out loud as you explain it, the way it says on the card. If your puzzle uses pigeonhole, say 'pigeonhole' and show both halves: the smaller number that can slip through with no repeat, and the one extra that forces one. If your puzzle uses parity, say 'what stays the same' and show the one count that never changes no matter what move happens.

problems.prompt: Peak 1, decimals: a number has a 7 in the tenths place, a 0 in the hundredths place, and a 4 in the thousandths place, with a 2 in the ones place. Write this number as a decimal.
explanation: Place value shift: build the number one place at a time, ones first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
That gives 2 in front of the point, then 7, then 0, then 4 after it: 2.704.
The 0 in the hundredths place cannot be skipped, or the 4 would land in the wrong place value.
problems.useAgain: when a decimal is described place by place and one of the middle places is a zero that cannot be skipped.
hints: Write the four digits in order: ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
A zero in a middle place still needs to be written, or the digits after it shift to the wrong place.
problems.socraticHint: If you left out the zero in the hundredths place, would the 4 still land in the thousandths place, or would it shift?

variant.prompt: A number has a 3 in the tenths place, a 0 in the hundredths place, and an 8 in the thousandths place, with a 5 in the ones place. Write this number as a decimal.

problems.prompt: Which of these correctly orders 0.099, 0.12 and 0.1 from smallest to largest?
explanation: Line up the decimals by place value: 0.099 has 0 tenths, 0.1 has 1 tenth, and 0.12 has 1 tenth too.
0.099 is smaller than both, since it has no tenths at all, only hundredths and thousandths.
Between 0.1 and 0.12, 0.1 is the same as 0.10, which is less than 0.12, so the order is 0.099, 0.1, 0.12.
problems.useAgain: when several decimals have different numbers of digits and you cannot just compare how long they look.
hints: Write every decimal with the same number of digits after the point before comparing, using extra zeros.
A decimal with more digits is not automatically bigger.
problems.socraticHint: Would writing 0.1 as 0.100 and 0.12 as 0.120 make it easier to compare them to 0.099 directly?

variant.prompt: Which of these correctly orders 0.11, 0.089 and 0.09 from smallest to largest?

explanation: Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left, the same as moving the decimal point one place to the right.
3.6 has the point between the 3 and the 6.
Move the point one place to the right: 36.
problems.useAgain: when you multiply a decimal by 10, 100 or 1000.
hints: Every zero in 10 moves the point one place.
Moving right makes the number bigger.
problems.socraticHint: When you multiply by 10, is it really the point that moves, or is it the digits sliding past a point that stays put?

problems.prompt: Notebooks cost $2.35 each. What is the total cost for 10 notebooks?
explanation: Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left, the same as moving the decimal point one place to the right.
2.35 has the point between the 2 and the 3.
Move the point one place to the right: 23.5, which is $23.50 in money.
problems.useAgain: when you multiply a price by 10.
hints: Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place.
Write the answer with two decimal places since it is money.
problems.socraticHint: Does multiplying a price by 10 change how many decimal places it needs, or just where the point sits among the digits it already has?

variant.prompt: Erasers cost $0.85 each. What is the total cost for 10 erasers?

problems.prompt: Summit: your mBot's turnTime variable starts at 0.3 seconds. Multiply it by 100, then divide that result by 1000. What decimal do you end with?
explanation: Chain the two shifts one at a time, left to right, just like the code would run them in order.
Multiplying by 100 shifts every digit two places to the left: 0.3 becomes 30.
Dividing by 1000 shifts every digit three places to the right: 30 becomes 0.03.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains more than one multiply-by-10-or-100 shift in a row.
hints: Do the two shifts one at a time, in the order the problem gives them.
Multiplying by 100 is two shifts right on the point; dividing by 1000 is three shifts left.
problems.socraticHint: If you multiplied by 100 and then divided by 100 again, right back where you started, would that tell you anything about how the two shifts in this problem compare in size?

variant.prompt: Summit: if turnTime started at 0.4 seconds, multiplied by 100, then divided by 1000, what decimal would you end with?

explanation: Of means times, so 3/4 of 60 is 3/4 x 60.
Divide 60 by 4 to get 15, the value of one fourth.
Multiply 15 by 3 to get 45, the value of three fourths.
problems.useAgain: when a problem asks for a fraction of an amount.
hints: Divide by the bottom number of the fraction first.
Multiply that result by the top number.
problems.socraticHint: Three fourths of a number is more than half of it but less than the whole thing: does your answer fall in that range?

problems.prompt: Summit: what is 6 divided by 3/4, all divided by 2/3?
explanation: Work left to right, one division at a time. First, 6 divided by 3/4: flip 3/4 to 4/3, and 6 times 4/3 is 8.
Now divide that result, 8, by 2/3: flip 2/3 to 3/2, and 8 times 3/2 is 12.
Two flip-and-multiply steps in a row, each one turning a division into an easier multiplication.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains more than one division by a fraction in a row.
hints: Work the two divisions one at a time, left to right.
Flip each fraction you divide by before multiplying, one step at a time.
problems.socraticHint: Dividing by a fraction smaller than one always makes a number bigger. After two such divisions in a row, should the final answer be much bigger than the 6 you started with, or only a little bigger?

variant.prompt: Summit: what is 8 divided by 2/3, all divided by 3/4?

problems.prompt: Peak 3, percent: write 35% as a fraction in simplest form.
explanation: Percent means out of one hundred, so 35% is 35/100.
Find the biggest number that divides evenly into both 35 and 100, that number is 5.
Divide the top and bottom by 5: 35/100 becomes 7/20.
problems.useAgain: when you need to turn a percent into a fraction.
hints: Write the percent as a number out of 100 first.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the same number.
problems.socraticHint: Why does turning a percent into a fraction always start with 100 on the bottom, even before you simplify anything?

variant.prompt: Write 45% as a fraction in simplest form.

explanation: Percent means out of one hundred, so 6% is 6/100.
6/100 as a decimal has the 6 in the hundredths place, two places after the point.
Write it as 0.06.
problems.useAgain: when you need to turn a percent into a decimal.
hints: Percent means out of one hundred.
Count two places after the decimal point for hundredths.
problems.socraticHint: Is 6% closer to one tenth of the whole, or one hundredth of it?

problems.prompt: Summit: a tablet costs $80. It is 20% off, then the store adds 5% sales tax, then you use a $10 gift card. How much do you actually pay?
explanation: Work through the three changes in order: discount first, then tax, then the gift card. Each one applies to the amount left after the step before it.
20% off means you pay 80% of the price: 80 times 0.8 is 64.
5% tax adds onto that new price: 64 times 1.05 is 67.20.
Last, take off the flat $10 gift card: 67.20 minus 10 is 57.20.
The trap is applying the tax or the gift card to the original $80 instead of the running total.
problems.useAgain: when a price changes three times in a row, like a discount, then a tax, then a flat coupon, and each step applies to the previous result.
hints: Work through the discount, then the tax, then the gift card, one at a time, always on the newest amount.
Only the very last step, the gift card, is a flat dollar amount instead of a percent.
problems.socraticHint: Of the three changes, discount, tax and gift card, which one is not a percent at all, and does that change when in the order you apply it?

variant.prompt: Summit: a backpack costs $60. It is 25% off, then the store adds 8% sales tax, then you use a $5 gift card. How much do you actually pay?

problems.prompt: At a party of 6 people, any two people either already know each other or are complete strangers. Prove that there must be 3 people at the party who all know each other, or 3 people who are all strangers to each other.

mustMention: pick one person and sort the other five into know or stranger
by pigeonhole at least three of them land in the same group
check whether any two of those three know each other; either way a matching triangle of three turns up

explanation: Pick one person at the party, call them Alex. Every other person either knows Alex or is a stranger to Alex, so sort the other five people into exactly those two groups.

Five people split only two ways. By pigeonhole, at least three of them land in the same group. Call three of them B, C and D. They all share one relationship with Alex, either all know Alex or all are strangers to Alex.
Now look at B, C and D among themselves. If two of them also share that same relationship, a triangle already exists: Alex plus that matching pair.
If instead no two of them share it, every pair among B, C and D must be the opposite relationship. That makes B, C and D themselves into a matching triangle of the other kind.

Either way, a party of 6 always forces one matching triangle, three who all know each other or three who are all strangers. This is a two way check. Test what happens when a pair matches, then test what happens when none do. Both paths land on a triangle.
problems.useAgain: when splitting people two ways guarantees a crowd on one side, and that guaranteed crowd is what the rest of a proof gets built on.
hints: Pick one person at the party and sort everyone else by their one relationship to that person: knows them, or a stranger to them. What does pigeonhole tell you about those two groups?
Once you have three people who share the same relationship with your first person, look only at those three. What happens if two of them share that relationship too? What happens if none of them do?
problems.socraticHint: Five people split two ways. What is the smallest number pigeonhole guarantees lands in one of those two groups?

variant.prompt: For the hungry: could a party of only 5 people always avoid having 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers? Draw 5 people in a circle, numbered 1 to 5, and say two people know each other exactly when they sit next to each other around the circle. Every other pair are strangers. Check that this party has no 3 people who all know each other and no 3 who are all strangers, and explain why that proves 6, not 5, is the smallest party size that always forces one.

mustMention: arrange the 5 people in a circle and let neighbors be the only friends
check that no three people around the circle are all mutual friends, and no three are all mutual strangers
since one arrangement of 5 people dodges both triangles, 5 is not enough and 6 is the smallest number that always works
